headline: High: agentic-flow can mutate shared state and use MCP, while python-cheatsheet is documentation-only, so the main risks are one-sided injection and compliance/data-flow issues rather than direct bidirectional conflict.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: agent_a can use MCP, stdin/stdout, and background workers, so if it ingests agent_b content through a shared channel, prompt injection is plausible. agent_b is documentation-only and has no execution or MCP surface, so it cannot actively inject back except via copied text. The pathway exists but is not default from the profiles alone.
conditions: IF agent_a is configured to read agent_b output from a shared file, clipboard, or MCP channel
IF operator copies agent_b text into agent_a as instructions
mitigations: Disable shared text channels between the agents
Wrap agent_b output in a non-executable template
Require explicit provenance tags before agent_a follows instructions
Review any MCP inputs for instruction-like content

B_data_leakage.rationale: agent_a touches code, repository metadata, learning patterns, performance metrics, and task prompts, while agent_b touches no data classes and has no filesystem or network surfaces. There is no documented shared workspace or upload path, so leakage from agent_a into agent_b is limited and mostly requires unusual manual bridging.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same sensitive workspace
IF operator manually transfers agent_a outputs into agent_b-facing documentation
mitigations: Keep the agents on separate workspaces
Avoid pasting agent_a outputs into agent_b artifacts
Strip secrets from agent_a logs before review
Use read-only exports for any handoff

C_capability_conflict.rationale: agent_a can execute shell, install packages, modify git state, and spawn subprocesses; agent_b cannot write files, modify git, or run subprocesses. Overlap is minimal, so direct capability conflict is unlikely unless an external orchestrator gives agent_b hidden write access not shown in its profile.
conditions: IF an external wrapper grants agent_b write or git privileges not listed in its profile
IF both are attached to the same mutable repo through another tool
mitigations: Keep agent_b read-only
Do not share a writable repository mount
Serialize any git operations through agent_a only
Add lockfiles around shared state changes

D_cascading_error.rationale: agent_a can produce analysis and modify git state, and agent_b is a content-writing agent that could render or reuse agent_a output. If agent_b treats agent_a output as authoritative, errors can cascade into published text or repo changes. The profiles do not show verification or critique safeguards, so the interaction is plausible in default use.
conditions: IF agent_b consumes agent_a output without a verification step
IF agent_a output is used as source material for published content or commits
mitigations: Insert a human verification step before reuse
Require citations for any factual claims from agent_a
Diff agent_a output against source material
Limit agent_b to drafting, not final publication

E_compliance.rationale: agent_a handles repository metadata and task prompts and can use MCP/GitHub, while agent_b is documentation-only with no data classes touched. No residency or regulated-data mismatch is documented, so compliance risk is mainly from accidental handling of sensitive repo content by agent_a rather than a pairwise policy conflict.
conditions: IF agent_a is given regulated data in its repository inputs
IF agent_b is used to publish content derived from restricted material
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of agent_a inputs
Use a separate publishing workflow for agent_b
Review retention settings on any MCP/GitHub integrations
Document data-class handling rules for both agents
